claim: The blind mole rat (Spalax ehrenbergi) is exceedingly solitary, territorial, and aggressive.
source: On the social scale, the blind mole rat (BMR; Spalax ehrenbergi) is an extreme. It is exceedingly solitary, territorial, and aggressive.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the behavioral characteristics of the BMR.

claim: BMRs reside underground in self-excavated tunnels that they rarely leave.
source: BMRs reside underground, in self-excavated tunnels that they rarely leave.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing the habitat of BMRs.

claim: BMRs possess specialized sensory systems for social communication and navigation.
source: They possess specialized sensory systems for social communication and navigation, which allow them to cope with the harsh environmental conditions underground.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characteristic of BMRs.

claim: Social isolation in prairie voles produces cardiovascular dysfunctions and depression.
source: Social isolation in prairie voles was shown to produce cardiovascular dysfunctions and depression (McNeal et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McNeal et al., 2014.

claim: Socially isolated male mice showed impaired GABAergic function and increased aggressiveness.
source: socially isolated male mice showed impaired GABAergic function and increased aggressiveness (Matsumoto et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsumoto et al., 2005.

claim: Out of 19 known subterranean rodent genera, 14 are solitary.
source: Interestingly, out of 19 known subterranean rodent genera, 14 are solitary (Nevo, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo, 1979.

claim: The naked mole-rat and Damaraland mole-rat are the only two known eusocial species within the Mammalia class.
source: the naked mole-rat (NMR; Heterocephalus glaber) and Damaraland mole-rat (Fukomys damarensis) are eusocial, residing in large underground communal colonies, and are in fact the only two known eusocial species within the Mammalia class (Bennett and Jarvis, 1988; Barker et al., 2021a; Figure 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Jarvis, 1988 and Barker et al., 2021a, and references Figure 1.

claim: BMRs weigh 100–250 g.
source: The BMR, weighing 100–250 g (Lacey et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lacey et al., 2001.

claim: BMRs can be found across a variety of habitats in the middle east.
source: can be found across a variety of habitats in the middle east (Nevo, 1961; Nevo, 1985)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nevo, 1961 and Nevo, 1985.

claim: BMRs have high longevity of 20 years or more.
source: high longevity of 20 years or more, and cancer resistance (Manov et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2017; Shams et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manov et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2017; Shams et al., 2005.

claim: BMRs exhibit cancer resistance.
source: high longevity of 20 years or more, and cancer resistance (Manov et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2017; Shams et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manov et al., 2013; Schmidt et al., 2017; Shams et al., 2005.

claim: Mice and rats are considered highly social animals.
source: Mice (Mus musculus) and rats (Rattus norvegicus), the most commonly used animal models in neuroscience (Ellenbroek and Youn, 2016), are considered highly social animals
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ellenbroek and Youn, 2016.

claim: Mice and rats are not suitable for answering scientific questions regarding mechanisms controlling naturally-occurring anti-social and solitary behaviors.
source: are considered highly social animals, and thus are not suitable for answering many scientific questions regarding the mechanisms controlling naturally-occurring anti-social and solitary behaviors.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the social nature of mice and rats.

claim: People diagnosed on the autism spectrum often present a decrease in socialization and increased aggressiveness.
source: For instance, people diagnosed on the autism spectrum, those who suffer from antisocial personality disorders, depression or neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's, often present a decrease in socialization and increased aggressiveness (Azevedo et al., 2020; Dutton and Karakanta, 2013; Gilley et al., 1997; Mazurek et al., 2013; Swearer et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: BMRs are seasonal breeders.
source: BMRs are seasonal breeders (Shanas et al., 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas et al., 1995.

claim: Male and female blind mole rats reside alone throughout the year, with the exception of short mating and lactating periods during the winter.
source: With the exception of short mating and lactating periods during the winter (the wet season), male and female blind mole rats reside alone throughout the year, patrolling their tunnels and defending their territories from conspecifics and congenerics (Nevo, 1961; Rado et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nevo, 1961 and Rado et al., 1993.

claim: Close encounters from territory encroachment are experienced as extremely stressful for BMRs and usually result in severe physiological stress and extreme aggression.
source: For the BMR, close encounters from territory encroachment are experienced as extremely stressful, and usually result in severe physiological stress and extreme aggression, frequently leading to the death of one or both individuals (Nevo, 1961; Nevo, 2013; Zuri et al., 1998b, Zuri and Terkel, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Agonistic and aggressive behaviors in BMRs are manifested by 'retreat and attack' postures and by 'bulldozing' a soil plug using the snout.
source: Agonistic and aggressive behaviors in BMRs are manifested by 'retreat and attack' postures and by 'bulldozing' a soil plug using the snout (Guttman et al., 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guttman et al., 1975.

claim: Aggressive gestures in BMRs include strong strikes and opponent-pushing with the head, open mouth sniffing and biting.
source: Other aggressive gestures include strong strikes and opponent-pushing with the head, open mouth sniffing (exposed incisors; Figure 4) and biting (Nevo et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1986 and references Figure 4.

claim: Aggressive behaviors in BMRs increase where there is more competition for resource availability.
source: These behaviors were shown to increase where there is more competition for resource availability (Nevo et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1982.

claim: Female BMRs present lower aggression intensity compared to males.
source: Females were reported to present lower aggression intensity compared to males (Nevo et al., 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1986.

claim: The behavioral component of aggressive behaviors in BMRs is independent of testosterone levels in males.
source: nevertheless, the behavioral component of these behaviors was shown to be independent of testosterone levels in male BMRs (Gottreich et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gottreich et al., 2001.

claim: BMRs engage in head drumming 'duets' back and forth across territories.
source: It has been noted that BMRs engage in head drumming 'duets' back and forth across territories (Rado et al., 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1987.

claim: The types of information encoded in BMR head drumming signals are not well understood.
source: but the types of information encoded in the signal (for example the signaler's level of dominance, sex, age, or individual identity) are not well understood (Randall, 2013; Seyfarth and Cheney, 2003; Tibbetts and Dale, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating the lack of understanding.

claim: Courtship in BMRs involves multimodal signaling including seismic head drums, vocal 'purrs' and olfactory cues, and engaging in tactile behaviors.
source: At a close distance to the female's tunnel, courtship ensues, involving multimodal signaling including seismic head drums, vocal 'purrs' and olfactory cues, and engaging in tactile behaviors until the female decides to mate with the male (Gazit and Terkel, 2000; Nevo, 1961; Nevo, 1969; Shanas et al., 1995; Figures 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and references to Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Copulatory pairs of BMRs spend brief periods together, retreating to their individual territories after mating.
source: Copulatory pairs spend brief periods together, retreating to their individual territories after mating (Gazit and Terkel, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 2000.

claim: Estrous female BMRs are able to discriminate chromosomal subspecies of male BMRs by their courtship calls.
source: It was observed that estrous females are able to discriminate chromosomal subspecies of male BMRs by their courtship calls, and that in most cases, estrous females would prefer the calls of their homospecific mates over those of heterospecific ones (Nevo et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1987.

claim: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days.
source: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days, after which the female delivers a litter of 3–4 pups on average (Gazit et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit et al., 1996.

claim: Female BMRs deliver a litter of 3–4 pups on average.
source: Gestation period in BMRs is 34 days, after which the female delivers a litter of 3–4 pups on average (Gazit et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit et al., 1996.

claim: Mother and pups in BMRs communicate by vocalizations in the first stages of ontogeny, and gradually shift to seismic communication of head drumming duets.
source: Mother and pups communicate by vocalizations in the first stages of ontogeny, and gradually shift to seismic communication of head drumming duets (Rado et al., 1991b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1991b.

claim: Mother BMRs show higher communication and aggression toward male pups compared to female pups prior to complete dispersal.
source: Interestingly, Gazit and Terkel, 1998 reported sex differences in mother-pup interactions prior to a complete dispersal, as mother's communication and aggression toward male pups was longer and more frequent compared to those toward female pups.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 1998.

claim: Dispersal of juvenile BMRs starts approximately 2 months after parturition.
source: This process leads to the gradual dispersal of the juveniles, starting approximately 2 months after parturition (Gazit and Terkel, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit and Terkel, 1998.

claim: Juvenile BMRs establish their own solitary territories at the age of approximately 3 months.
source: and ending in the individual establishment of their own solitary territories at the age of approximately 3 months (Rado et al., 1991b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1991b.

claim: BMRs integrate photoperiodic changes and entrain a circadian activity rhythm by light received through their atrophied eyes.
source: Despite residing almost exclusively underground, BMRs were shown to integrate photoperiodic changes and entrain a circadian activity rhythm by light received through their atrophied eyes (see section 'Circadian rhythm')
evidence: This claim references another section of the manuscript for supporting evidence.

claim: In male prairie voles, alteration of both temperature and photoperiod caused regression in synthesis of gonadotropin-releasing hormone and in their reproductive function.
source: In male prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster), alteration of both temperature and photoperiod caused regression in synthesis of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, and in their reproductive function (Kriegsfeld et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kriegsfeld et al., 2001.

claim: BMRs are generalists that forage and cache encountered food items, such as geophytes and herbaceous plants.
source: BMRs are generalists that forage and cache encountered food items, such as geophytes and herbaceous plants (Galil, 1967; Heth, 1989, Lövy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: BMR foraging and food-caching behaviors are essential to ensure survival throughout the year.
source: The BMR's foraging and food-caching behaviors are essential to ensure survival throughout the year (Rado et al., 1993; Vleck, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rado et al., 1993 and Vleck, 1979.

claim: In the summer, BMRs stay largely inactive in tunnels at deeper and cooler depths (>40 cm).
source: In the summer, individuals stay largely inactive in tunnels at deeper and cooler depths (>40 cm) (Rado et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1993.

claim: BMRs have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster.
source: BMRs were shown to have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster, and retaining 45% of their performance 120 days later (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claim: BMRs retain 45% of their maze performance 120 days later.
source: BMRs were shown to have far superior spatial memories compared to rats, learning a maze significantly faster, and retaining 45% of their performance 120 days later (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claim: BMR tunnels can be as long as 100 m.
source: While it is unclear how many food caches BMRs may have branching off their tunnels, which can be as long as 100 m
evidence: This is stated as a fact about BMR tunnel length.

claim: BMRs possess rudimentary eyes less than 1 mm in diameter that are covered by furred skin.
source: While blind mole rats appear as if they have no eyes, they do possess rudimentary eyes (less than 1 mm in diameter), that are covered by furred skin (Cooper et al., 1993b, Haim et al., 1983; ; Rado et al., 1992; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and references Figure 2.

claim: The lens of the BMR is degenerated and embedded within a hypertrophied harderian gland.
source: The lens of the BMR is degenerated and embedded within a hypertrophied harderian gland (Cooper et al., 1993b, Haim et al., 1983; Rado et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The BMR's retina contains < 900 ganglion cells.
source: The BMR's retina contains < 900 ganglion cells (Cooper et al., 1993a)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 1993a.

claim: Rat retinas contain >50,000 ganglion cells.
source: a significantly low number compared to >50,000 cells found in rats, for example (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2016.

claim: Brain structures involved in image processing are severely regressed and dysfunctional in the BMR.
source: Moreover, brain structures involved in image processing are severely regressed and dysfunctional in the BMR (Cooper et al., 1993a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cooper et al., 1993a.

claim: The dorsal lateral geniculate body in BMRs is strongly activated by auditory stimuli.
source: For instance, the dorsal lateral geniculate body, which is the primary visual nuclei in the thalamus of sighted mammals, that sends visual information to the visual cortex, was reported to be strongly activated by auditory stimuli in BMRs (Bronchti et al., 2002; Bronchti et al., 1989; Heil et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The BMR's retina lacks short-wave opsine cones.
source: Although the BMR's retina lacks short-wave opsine cones (David-Gray et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to David-Gray et al., 2002.

claim: The BMR's retina includes at least three types of photoreceptors (rodopsin, coneopsin and L/M cone opsin).
source: it includes at least three types of photoreceptors (rodopsin, coneopsin and L/M cone opsin) that collect the scant light penetrating the soil (Burda, 2006; David-Gray et al., 1999; Esquiva et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Light induces gene expression in the BMR's suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: Therefore, despite being blind, light induces gene expression in the SCN (Vuillez et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vuillez et al., 1994.

claim: Light entrains circadian rhythms of locomotor behavior in the BMR.
source: and entrains circadian rhythms of locomotor behavior in the BMR (David-Gray et al., 1998; Rado et al., 1991a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to David-Gray et al., 1998 and Rado et al., 1991a.

claim: Enucleation abolished light-induced reactions in BMRs.
source: These reactions to light rely upon retinal photoreceptors, since enucleation abolished them (David-Gray et al., 1998; Pevet et al., 1984; Rado et al., 1991a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The BMR's harderian gland is able to synthesize melatonin.
source: In addition to the atrophied eyes, the BMR's harderian gland is also involved in photoperiodic perception, as it is able to synthesize melatonin (Balemans et al., 1980)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Balemans et al., 1980.

claim: The BMR's harderian gland is involved in photoperiodic detection.
source: and it was shown to be involved in photoperiodic detection (Pevet et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pevet et al., 1984.

claim: Melatonin receptors were found in the BMR's harderian gland.
source: Melatonin receptors were also found in the BMR's harderian gland, and were suggested to take part in a negative feedback control of melatonin production (Gilad et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gilad et al., 1997.

claim: The eusocial, subterranean Damaraland mole-rat possesses a circadian melatonin rhythm that is modulated according to photoperiodic changes.
source: Interestingly, the eusocial, subterranean Damaraland mole-rat was also shown to possess a circadian melatonin rhythm that is modulated according to photoperiodic changes (Richter et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2006.

claim: Blind mole rats have magnetoreception abilities.
source: Kimchi and Terkel, 2001 demonstrated that blind mole rats have magnetoreception abilities, and that they rely on them when choosing the locations for their nests and food caches.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claim: When shifting the polarity of the earth's magnetic field by 180̊, BMRs shifted the location of their preferred nest and food cache sites accordingly.
source: When shifting the polarity of the earth's magnetic field by 180̊, BMRs shifted the location of their preferred nest and food cache sites accordingly (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claim: Following surgical removal of their eyes, individual Ansell's mole-rat demonstrated impaired magnetic sensing.
source: In addition, following surgical removal of their eyes, individual Ansell's mole-rat (Fukomys anselli) demonstrated impaired magnetic sensing, supporting the hypothesis that in mole rats, magnetoreception receptors are located in the cornea (Caspar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caspar et al., 2020.

claim: Experiments on BMR magnetoreception were conducted in total darkness.
source: However, some observations in BMRs suggest that the their magnetoreception is independent of light, as experiments were conducted in total darkness (Kimchi and Terkel, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2001.

claim: The Zambian mole rat's perception of the earth's magnetic field is independent of light.
source: This finding is supported by a study of another mole rat species, the Zambian mole rat (Fukomys amatus), that was shown to be independent of light in its perception of the earth's magnetic field (Marhold et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Marhold et al., 1997.

claim: Fossorial and subterranean animals generally hear better at low frequencies and have restricted hearing ranges, compared to surface-dwelling rodents.
source: Accordingly, fossorial and subterranean animals generally hear better at low frequencies and have restricted hearing ranges, compared to surface-dwelling rodents that have been known to produce frequencies as high as in the ultrasonic range (Dent et al., 2018; He et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dent et al., 2018 and He et al., 2021.

claim: The Highveld mole rat is more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz).
source: The Highveld mole rat (Müller and Burda, 1989) and the Zambian mole rat (Brückmann and Burda, 1997), both subterranean rodents, are more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Müller and Burda, 1989.

claim: The Zambian mole rat is more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz).
source: The Highveld mole rat (Müller and Burda, 1989) and the Zambian mole rat (Brückmann and Burda, 1997), both subterranean rodents, are more sensitive to very low frequencies (0.8 kHz)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brückmann and Burda, 1997.

claim: The surface-dwelling feral house mouse is most sensitive to higher frequencies (16 kHz).
source: while the surface-dwelling feral house mouse (Heffner and Masterton, 1980) is most sensitive to higher frequencies (16 kHz).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Masterton, 1980.

claim: Peak sensitivity in the surface-dwelling guinea pig is –9 dB SPL.
source: For example, peak sensitivity in the surface-dwelling guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) is –9 dB SPL (sound pressure level) (Prosen et al., 1978)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prosen et al., 1978.

claim: Peak sensitivity in the subterranean naked mole rat is 35 dB SPL.
source: while in the subterranean naked mole rat it is just 35 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1993.

claim: Trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitude of 60 dB SPL.
source: Results from behavioral audiograms showed that trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitute of 60 dB SPL , with peak sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: Blind mole rats have peak hearing sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL.
source: Results from behavioral audiograms showed that trained blind mole rats can hear between 54 Hz and 5.6 kHz at an amplitute of 60 dB SPL , with peak sensitivity at 1 kHz at 32 dB SPL (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: Blind mole rats have poor sound localization abilities.
source: Additionally, blind mole rats have poor sound localization abilities, as demonstrated from playback of left and right speakers with 180o of separation (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration.
source: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration, and performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2ms (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: Blind mole rats performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2 ms.
source: Blind mole rats cannot localize signals less than 400 ms in duration, and performed best at localizing sound bursts of 1.2ms (Heffner and Heffner, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heffner and Heffner, 1992.

claim: The BMR lacks an external pinna of the outer ear.
source: The lower hearing sensitivity and minimal localization ability are apparent in the morphology of the BMR, which lacks an external pinna of the outer ear (see ear opening location in Figure 2).
evidence: This claim references Figure 2 for visual evidence.

claim: The BMR's middle and inner ear are uniquely structured, creating inefficient transmission of airborne sound.
source: The BMR's middle and inner ear are uniquely structured, creating inefficient transmission of airborne sound (Rado et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1989.

claim: Giant mole rats have a repertoire of 14 call types as determined by behavioral context and spectro-temporal features.
source: Giant mole rats (Fukomys mechowii) were demonstrated to have a repertoire of 14 call types as determined by behavioral context, such as teeth-fencing and predator alarm, and by spectro-temporal features (Bednářová et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bednářová et al., 2013.

claim: Giant mole rat calls have peak frequencies of less than 5 kHz.
source: In accordance with their low frequency hearing ranges, these calls are low in frequency, with peak frequencies of less than 5 kHz (Bednářová et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bednářová et al., 2013.

claim: The eusocial naked mole rat has dialects in the 'soft chirp' call type across colonies that signifies group membership.
source: The eusocial naked mole rat was recently shown to have dialects in the 'soft chirp' call type across colonies that signifies group membership (Barker et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barker et al., 2021b.

claim: At least six call types determined by behavioral context, all with frequencies below 8 kHz, have been noted in BMRs.
source: At least six call types determined by behavioral context, all with frequencies below 8 kHz, have been noted thus far (Capranica et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Capranica et al., 1974.

claim: Different call types in BMRs are used to facilitate mother and pup communication.
source: Different call types are used to facilitate mother and pup communication (Capranica et al., 1974; Gazit and Terkel, 1998; Rado et al., 1991b)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different call types in BMRs are used in male courtship displays during the mating season.
source: and used in male courtship displays during the mating season (Gazit and Terkel, 2000; Nevo, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gazit and Terkel, 2000 and Nevo, 1969.

claim: BMR courtship calls differ in frequency and temporal components across the Spalax chromosomal subspecies.
source: These courtship calls differ in frequency and temporal components across the Spalax chromosomal subspecies, and appear to play a role in assortative mating between the neighboring populations (Heth et al., 1988; Nevo et al., 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1988 and Nevo et al., 1987.

claim: Distress calls in BMRs have peak frequencies between 4 and 6 kHz.
source: Distress calls with peak frequencies between 4 and 6 kHz have also been opportunistically observed in lab studies (Bronchti et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bronchti et al., 1989.

claim: A BMR produces vibrational signals by drumming on the ceiling of its tunnel with the large, flattened portion of its head, producing bursts of head drums (approx. 2–4 drums per burst, 0.3 s duration).
source: A BMR produces vibrational signals by drumming on the ceiling of its tunnel with the large, flattened portion of its head, producing bursts of head drums (approx. 2–4 drums per burst, 0.3 s duration) (Heth et al., 1987; Rado et al., 1987; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1987 and Rado et al., 1987, and references Figure 4.

claim: BMR seismic signals range in the frequency of approximately 100–250 Hz and may travel as far as 10 m or more.
source: Seismic signals range in the frequency of approximately 100–250 Hz and may travel as far as 10 m or more (Heth et al., 1987; Rado et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1987 and Rado et al., 1987.

claim: BMRs perceive seismic signals by pressing the side of their lower jaw against the tunnel wall, which transmits the signals to the inner ear by means of bone conduction.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mason et al., 2010 and Rado et al., 1989, and references Figure 4A.

claim: BMRs perceive seismic signals via mechanoreceptors located on their paws.
source: The Second is via mechanoreceptors located on their paws (Kimchi et al., 2005).

claim: Providing a vibration stimulus in contact with the lower jaw evoked responses in the auditory brainstem of BMRs.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1998.

claim: Bilaterally deafened BMRs showed loss of response to vibration stimuli and eventual ceasing of head drumming behavior in the course of 4–6 weeks.
source: Providing a vibration stimulus in contact with the lower jaw evoked responses in the auditory brainstem, and bilaterally deafened mole rats, showed loss of response and eventual ceasing of head drumming behavior in the course of 4–6 weeks (Rado et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rado et al., 1998.

claim: The occipital cortex in BMRs is activated by frequencies corresponding to both vibrational and acoustic signals.
source: Furthermore, the occipital cortex, usually associated with vision, was shown to be activated by frequencies corresponding to both vibrational and acoustic signals (Bronchti et al., 2002; Heil et al., 1991; Sadka and Wollberg, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Two clusters of cells in the BMR cortex fired in response to frequencies centered around 2.5–4.4 kHz, matching airborne social vocalizations, and to 100 Hz, matching the frequency of long-distance vibratory signals.
source: Specifically, two clusters of cells fired in response to frequencies centered around 2.5–4.4 kHz, matching airborne social vocalizations, and to 100 Hz, matching the frequency of long-distance vibratory signals (Sadka and Wollberg, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadka and Wollberg, 2004.

claim: The BMR's somatosensory cortex extends far into the occipital cortex.
source: In addition to the auditory cortex, it was further shown that the BMR's somatosensory cortex also extends far into the occipital cortex (Necker et al., 1992; Rehkämper et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Necker et al., 1992 and Rehkämper et al., 1994.

claim: The somatosensory system in the isocortex of the blind mole rat is 1.7 times larger compared to the laboratory rat, when taking into consideration the differences in body weight and brain size.
source: The somatosensory system in the isocortex of the blind mole rat was shown to be 1.7 times larger compared to the laboratory rat, when taking into consideration the differences in body weight and brain size of the two species (Mann et al., 1997).

claim: The dermal papillae of the rhinarium in the BMR contains a few Merkel cell-axon complexes and simple Meissner's corpuscles.
source: Klauer and colleagues found that the dermal papillae of the rhinarium in the BMR contains a few Merkel cell-axon complexes and simple Meissner's corpuscles.
evidence: This claim is attributed to Klauer and colleagues in the text.

claim: BMRs consistently engage in a 'wall seeking' behavior during maze learning and exploration tasks.
source: During maze learning and exploration tasks, BMRs consistently engage in a 'wall seeking' behavior, in which they press their bodies against the side of the wall, sometimes alternating sides, and brushing the vibrissae against the maze surfaces (Kimchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2004.

claim: Blind mole rats performed significantly better in a narrow maze which allowed constant contact with the wall, compared to a maze twice the width of their body diameter.
source: When comparing maze learning and performance, blind mole rats performed significantly better in a narrow maze which allowed constant contact with the wall, compared to a maze twice the width of their body diameter (Kimchi and Terkel, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2000.

claim: Rats performed better in the wider maze compared to the narrow maze.
source: In contrast, rats performed better in the wider maze (Kimchi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2004.

claim: BMRs dig their tunnels to exactly the diameter of their own body width.
source: In nature, BMRs dig their tunnels to exactly the diameter of their own body width, in order to obtain maximal tactile information (Kimchi and Terkel, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi and Terkel, 2002.

claim: For naked mole rats, the incisors are represented in approximately 31% of the somatosensory cortex.
source: Additionally, for naked mole rats which use their teeth for digging, foraging, social encounters, and moving pups, the incisors are represented in approximately 31% of the somatosensory cortex (Catania and Remple, 2002; Park et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Catania and Remple, 2002 and Park et al., 2007.

claim: BMRs use seismic signaling as an echolocation behavior.
source: Kimchi and colleagues demonstrated that BMRs use seismic signaling as an echolocation behavior (Kimchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claim: In field experiments, blind mole rats were able to detect obstacles placed by researchers in their tunnels and repeatedly dug around or over them.
source: In field experiments, blind mole rats were able to detect obstacles placed by the researchers in their tunnels (various size ditches), and repeatedly dug around or over them.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from field experiments.

claim: The bypass strategy of BMRs varied depending on the size of the obstacle.
source: The bypass strategy varied depending on the size of the obstacle (large/small ditches), likely to minimize energetic costs (Kimchi and Terkel, 2003a, Kimchi and Terkel, 2003b; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimchi and Terkel, 2003a and 2003b, and references Figure 3C.

claim: Head drums used for echolocation in BMRs are higher in frequency (250–300 Hz) and produced as a single hit rather than bursts at intervals of approximately 8 s.
source: Unlike head drums used for intraspecific communication, these drums were higher in frequency (250–300 Hz) and produced as a single hit rather than bursts at intervals of approximately 8 s (Kimchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claim: The amplitude and frequency of the wavelengths recorded by geophones are sufficient for rapid detection of reflected waves when the BMR is 30–50 cm away from an obstacle.
source: Through modeling, it was demonstrated that the amplitude and frequency of the wavelengths recorded by geophones are sufficient for rapid detection of reflected waves when the individual is 30–50 cm away from an obstacle (Kimchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claim: BMRs can detect seismic signals produced by a mechanical shaker or a stimulus mole rat via their paws.
source: Experimentally, it was shown that BMRs can detect seismic signals produced by a mechanical shaker or a stimulus mole rat, also via their paws (Kimchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimchi et al., 2005.

claim: The glabrous skin of the front and hind feet of the BMR contains 15–20 lamellated Pacinian corpuscles.
source: The glabrous (hairless) skin of the front and hind feet of the BMR contains 15–20 lamellated Pacinian corpuscles, a type of mechanoreceptor known to be sensitive to high-frequency vibrations from 10 to 400 Hz in mammals (Kimchi et al., 2005; McIntyre, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimchi et al., 2005 and McIntyre, 1980.

claim: BMRs have been shown to use olfaction to discriminate poisonous versus edible food items from the plant growth hormones, kairomones located within soil where plants had been growing.
source: BMRs have been shown to use olfaction to discriminate poisonous versus edible food items from the plant growth hormones, kairomones located within soil where plants had been growing (Heth et al., 1992, Heth et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heth et al., 1992 and 2002.

claim: BMRs possess dorsoventrally flattened, wide snouts (~15 mm wide in adults).
source: BMRs possess dorsoventrally flattened, wide, snouts (~15 mm wide in adults; personal observations) (Figure 2)
evidence: This claim is based on personal observations and references Figure 2.

claim: The VNO of the blind mole rat opens directly to the nasal cavity by a narrow canal, and is not connected to the oral cavity.
source: As in rats (Addison and Rademaker, 1927), the VNO of the blind mole rat opens directly to the nasal cavity by a narrow canal, and is not connected to the oral cavity (Zuri et al., 1998a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zuri et al., 1998a.

claim: In developing BMRs from infancy to adulthood, there is an approximately 8.5-fold increase in VNO length (from 1.5 mm at 4 days to 13 mm in adults).
source: In developing mole rats from infancy to adulthood, there is an approximately 8.5-fold increase in VNO length (from 1.5 mm at 4 days to 13 mm in adults) (Zuri et al., 1998a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zuri et al., 1998a.

claim: African mole rat species show postnatal vomeronasal epithelium (VNE) length increase of less than one-fold.
source: This increase is much more substantial when compared to findings in African mole rat species (family Bathyergidae), which show postnatal vomeronasal epithelium (VNE) length increase of less than one-fold (Dennis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dennis et al., 2020.

claim: In the naked mole rat, no postnatal volumetric growth was found in the VNE.
source: Moreover, in the naked mole rat, no postnatal volumetric growth was found in the VNE (Smith et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2007.

claim: There has been a convergent reduction of V1Rs in different subterranean rodents, including the BMR.
source: Recently, it was shown that there has been a convergent reduction of V1Rs in different subterranean rodents, including the BMR (Jiao et al., 2019; Zhao, 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiao et al., 2019 and Zhao, 2021.

claim: The BMR secretes pheromones from the large harderian gland located at the ocular orbit by self-grooming.
source: The BMR secretes pheromones from the large harderian gland located at the ocular orbit by self-grooming (Shanas and Terkel, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas and Terkel, 1995.

claim: The harderian gland in BMRs is sexually dimorphic in lipid and volatile composition, and in size and weight (larger in males).
source: The harderian gland is sexually dimorphic in lipid and volatile composition, and in size and weight (larger in males) (Shanas and Terkel, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas and Terkel, 1999.

claim: Harderian gland size and weight in BMRs correlate with total body mass and season of the year.
source: Gland size and weight also correlate with total body mass and season of the year (Shanas and Terkel, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas and Terkel, 1999.

claim: Secretion of pheromones by grooming during social interactions in BMRs is thought to signal submissiveness and appeasement.
source: Secretion of pheromones by grooming during social interactions is thought to signal submissiveness and appeasement (Shanas and Terkel, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas and Terkel, 1997.

claim: Male BMRs use urine and feces for scent marking, to proclaim their territories and prevent intrusion by competitors.
source: Male BMRs use urine and feces for scent marking, to proclaim their territories and prevent intrusion by competitors (Gazit et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gazit et al., 1997.

claim: Specific pheromones in urine are important for both courtship and territoriality in male and female BMRs.
source: However, mole rat odors may also serve as sexual attractants. Heth and colleagues showed that specific pheromones in urine are important for both courtship and territoriality in males and females (Heth et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heth et al., 1992.

claim: Female BMRs are attracted to males with high urinary testosterone levels.
source: A later study showed that female BMRs were attracted to males with high urinary testosterone levels, suggesting that testosterone and androstenedione behave as pheromones and have an olfactory effect (Gottreich et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gottreich et al., 2000.

claim: Male BMRs kept in a lab facility have significantly lower androgens, testosterone and androstenedione levels compared to male BMRs in the wild.
source: Follow-up studies showed that male BMRs kept in a lab facility have significantly lower androgens, testosterone and androstenedione levels compared to male BMRs in the wild, which might explain their low courtship behavior in the lab and the low breeding success rate in captivity (Shanas et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shanas et al., 1995.

claim: Artificially induced estrous female mole rats are attracted to, and prefer male odors belonging to their chromosomal subspecies when auditory and tactile cues are excluded.
source: Artificially induced estrous female mole rats were shown to be attracted to, and prefer male odors belonging to their chromosomal subspecies when auditory and tactile cues were excluded (Nevo et al., 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nevo et al., 1976.

claim: In the eusocial NMR and African Ansell's mole rat, the majority of OT cells was found in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON).
source: In the eusocial NMR (Rosen et al., 2008) and African Ansell's mole rat (Valesky et al., 2012), the majority of OT cells was found in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON), similar to many other mammalian species (Buijs, 1978; Dubois-Dauphin et al., 1989; Hermes et al., 1988; Sofroniew et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: No sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in prairie voles.
source: However, no sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in prairie voles (Yamamoto et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamamoto et al., 2004.

claim: No sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in Ansell's mole rats.
source: However, no sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in prairie voles (Yamamoto et al., 2004), Ansell's mole rats (Valesky et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Valesky et al., 2012.

claim: No sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in naked mole rats.
source: However, no sexual dimorphism in OT neuron number was found in prairie voles (Yamamoto et al., 2004), Ansell's mole rats (Valesky et al., 2012), and naked mole rats (Mooney and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mooney and Holmes, 2013.

claim: When considering the differences in brain size, the BMR's PVN contains significantly lower numbers of OT neurons compared to mice.
source: Preliminary data recently established in a comparative study in our lab, found that when considering the differences in brain size, the BMR's PVN contains significantly lower numbers of OT neurons compared to mice.
evidence: This claim is based on preliminary unpublished data from the authors' lab.

claim: There is no indication of sex differences in the number of OT cells in the PVN of male and female BMRs.
source: Furthermore, we found no indication of sex differences in the number of OT cells in the PVN of male and female BMRs (unpublished data).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Subordinate naked mole rats have more OT-producing neurons in the PVN compared to breeding individuals.
source: a study of the eusocial NMR that examined the effect of social status on the number of OT neurons, revealed that subordinate individuals have more OT-producing neurons in the PVN compared to breeding individuals (Mooney and Holmes, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mooney and Holmes, 2013.

claim: Peripheral administration of OT to the eusocial naked mole rat enhanced social behaviors such as in-colony huddling, time spent in close proximity to a conspecific and the number of its investigations.
source: Peripheral administration of OT to the eusocial naked mole rat enhanced social behaviors such as in-colony huddling, time spent in close proximity to a conspecific and the number of its investigations, and this enhancement was blocked by co-administration of an OT antagonist (Mooney et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mooney et al., 2014.

claim: No significant differences in OT and AVP neurons were found in individuals from different social and reproductive ranks in the African Ansell's mole rat.
source: As for the African Ansell's mole rat, no significant differences in OT and AVP neurons were found in individuals from different social and reproductive ranks (Valesky et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Valesky et al., 2012.

claim: Shank3b KO mice, a common mouse model of ASD, have reduced numbers of OT neurons in the PVN.
source: For example, it was recently shown that Shank3b KO mice, a common mouse model of ASD, which present abnormal social behaviors, have reduced numbers of OT neurons in the PVN (Resendez et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Resendez et al., 2020.

claim: Enhanced aggression due to early life stress (ES) is associated with upregulation of AVP expression in the PVN and SON of male rats.
source: For example, enhanced aggression due to early life stress (ES) was shown to be associated with upregulation of AVP expression in the PVN and SON of male rats (Veenema et al., 2006; Veenema and Neumann, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Veenema et al., 2006 and Veenema and Neumann, 2009.

claim: Mice and mandarin voles presented decreased aggression after ES, which was accompanied by a decrease in AVP neurons in the PVN.
source: On the contrary, mice (Tsuda et al., 2011) and mandarin voles (Wei et al., 2013) presented decreased aggression after ES, which was accompanied by a decrease in AVP neurons in the PVN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsuda et al., 2011 and Wei et al., 2013.

claim: Considerable differences in CRF abundance and receptor binding in the telencephalon exist between the eusocial NMR and the solitary Cape mole rat.
source: In a comparative study, Coen found considerable differences in CRF abundance and receptor binding in the telencephalon, between the eusocial NMR and the solitary Cape mole rat (Coen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coen et al., 2015.

claim: Being congenitally blind, Spalax ehrenbergi is deprived of visual inputs, and thus compensates via the diversion of the visual modality to the auditory modality.
source: Being congenitally blind, Spalax ehrenbergi is deprived of visual inputs, and thus compensates via the diversion of the visual modality to the auditory modality.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the BMR.

claim: There is no known way to determine the age of an adult BMR captured in the field.
source: To our knowledge, there is no known way to determine the age of an adult BMR captured in the field, which adds to the uncontrolled variables involved in BMR research.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in BMR research.

claim: A Spalax ehrenbergi genomic assembly has been deposited for a single female BMR.
source: A Spalax ehrenbergi genomic assembly has been deposited for a single female BMR (Fang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fang et al., 2014.

claim: Transcriptomic sequencing analyses have uncovered differential expression profiles in BMRs under different conditions related to underground stressors.
source: In addition, transcriptomic sequencing analyses have uncovered differential expression profiles in BMRs under different conditions related to underground stressors (Fang et al., 2014; Malik et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fang et al., 2014 and Malik et al., 2011.

claim: scRNA sequencing of microglia revealed similarities of BMRs to other rodents.
source: and scRNA sequencing of microglia revealed similarities of BMRs to other rodents (Geirsdottir et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Geirsdottir et al., 2019.

claim: A successful transformation of NMR cells has been reported using a novel CRISPR gRNA library and lentiviral vectors.
source: Recently, Hadi and colleagues demonstrated a promising breakthrough in the field of genetic engineering in mole rats, reporting a successful transformation of NMR cells, using a novel CRISPR gRNA library and lentiviral vectors (Hadi, 2020a; Hadi et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hadi, 2020a and Hadi et al., 2020b.
